summary: This RFC defines a Telnet option for passing a 64-bit terminal location number, from a system created at CMU to find where a user is logged in from. It is a proposed standard.

eli5.summary: A number that tells the computer where in the building you are sitting, so people can find you or phone you.

subtitle: A Telnet option that passes a compact 64-bit number saying which terminal on which host a user is connecting from.

tldr.problem: For an incoming network connection a host sees only the remote host's name, but systems often want to know where a user is sitting, to find or phone them.
tldr.mechanism: The TTYLOC option, code 28, sends a 64-bit number made of a 32-bit Internet host address and a 32-bit terminal number in a subnegotiation after WILL and DO agree.
tldr.outcome: It is a shorthand for communities that share facilities, such as CMU, and is not a replacement for the SEND-LOCATION option of RFC 779.

today: The unit metadata lists RFC 946 as a Proposed Standard, and no RFC is recorded as obsoleting or updating it.

sections.title: Why Send a Terminal Location
sections.content:
Many systems can tell where a user is logged in from, often including a telephone extension or office occupant names. That helps with physically locating people or calling them. For incoming network connections only the remote host's name is available, so this option and the Telnet Terminal Location option (RFC 779) give the system that information. The system can then pass it to tools such as FINGER and WHOIS.

In March of 1982, CMU built a terminal location database based on its PUP-based network, using a 64-bit number called the Terminal Location Number or TTYLOC. CMU wanted to extend it to the TCP-based networking replacing PUP. The number is cheap to store and to pass between layers, while sending a location string of unfixed length looked expensive.
sections.eli5: When someone calls from another building, a number can tell you which desk they are at.

sections.title: The TTYLOC Number
sections.content:
The TTYLOC number is 64 bits, made of two 32-bit numbers. One is the official ARPA Internet host address (any one of them for a multi-homed host). The other is a number for the terminal on that host.

A host address of 0.0.0.0 means unknown. A terminal number of FFFFFFFF (hex) means unknown, and FFFFFFFE means detached, for processes not attached to a terminal. Bytes go from most significant to least significant.
sections.eli5: The number has two halves: which building, and which desk inside it. Special values mean unknown or not at a desk.

sections.title: Commands and Negotiation
sections.content:
The option is TTYLOC, code 28. WILL offers or confirms sending the information, and DO requests or confirms receiving it. WON'T and DON'T refuse, and by default the information is neither sent nor received. The data goes in IAC SB TTYLOC <format> <number> IAC SE, with IAC doubling, and the 64-bit number uses format 0.

The user Telnet can start with WILL TTYLOC and the server answers DO TTYLOC, or the server can start with DO and the user answers WILL. Either way the user then sends the number. If sending the TTYLOC number is refused, it is recommended to try the Telnet Terminal Location option (SEND-LOCATION in RFC 779).
sections.eli5: The computers ask each other if they want to share the desk number, and only then is it sent.
